catalog_quote: As a general rule, stress is penultimate in J.Dohok. Lexical stress is characterised by an increase in intensity, and frequently also in pitch. If the accented syllable is open, moreover, the vowel is long, unless this is [ə] (typically above 95ms). [...] There is, however, a number of exception to these rules; these are discussed below. (p. 79) [...] First, as a general rule, stress is penultimate. There are three types of reason due to which lexical stress sometimes cannot be penultimate; the necessary conditions blocking penultimate stress are most commonly manifested in verbs and forms with the enclitic copula and mostly involve morphemes which cannot take stress. [...] In the verbal forms, the semi-clitic L-suffixes (subject- or object-indexing) and the -wa suffix cannot take stress. In such cases, accent falls as close to the penultimate syllable as possible, for instance, on the syllable before an L-suffix and/or wa if these morphemes are penultimate (Hoberman 1997, 331) (Rule 1a). (pp. 81-82) [...] In contrast to other verbal forms, in the imperative, lexical stress is fixed on the first syllable (Rule 1c) in J. Dohok, as case in many other NENA dialects. (p. 89)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable by default (stressed open-syllable vowels are long). Certain morphemes cannot carry stress: the semi-clitic L-suffixes and past -wa in verbs (stress then lands as close to the penult as possible, i.e. on the syllable preceding them), the enclitic present copula (invisible to stress, so stress stays on the penult of the host), and the 2pl -etun keeps stress on its first syllable; a general verbal rule (after Khan) is that stress must stay on a syllable containing a radical of the verbal base. Imperatives have fixed initial stress. Molin's Figure 2 (spectrogram of ḥakoma) shows the stressed syllable with highest intensity and pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 82: when stress cannot be penultimate, the open penultimate vowel is lengthened; 'This type of prominence can be considered secondary stress' (Rule 2). Same lengthening applies before an enclitic copula (p. 88).
new_statements.exceptions: L-suffixes and -wa cannot take stress (stress retracts, e.g. garšà-li 'she may pull me', šqə́llōxun 'you pl. took'); enclitic 3rd-person copula invisible to stress (gúrgā=le); 2pl -etun keeps stress on its first syllable (garšétun, garšə́tū-le); imperatives stressed on the first syllable (mšádər-re 'send it!'); adapted loanwords with non-penult stress noted p. 80 (ḥàmmam, kundắra); occasional retraction to the antepenult near the end of intonation units (Molin 2020 p. 121 fn 21). Trans-Zab Jewish dialects (not LD) are noted as tending to word-final stress (p. 12).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress, described separately from intonation-unit nucleus stress (§2.4, p. 94); instrumental durations given for vowels. The cross-dialect claim that Rule 1a holds for the other LD dialects (p. 82 fn 13) is Molin's inference from Hoberman 1997 (J. Amedia), Mutzafi 2008a p. 30 (J. Betanure) and Fassberg 2010 p. 34 (J. Challa).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Jewish dialect of Dohok (J. Dohok), one town-dialect of the Lishana Deni cluster (Glottolog lish1247; no separate glottocode for Dohok). Molin explicitly lists Zakho, Amedia, Betanure, Nerwa, Aradhin, Atrush, Challa and Gzira as the other members of the cluster (thesis p. 4-5) and states that the L-suffix stress rule is 'apparently also' valid for the other LD dialects (p. 82 fn 13). For Zakho proper the only opened statement is Aloni 2022 p. 276 fn 142 ('NENA phonology here: ḥ>x, penultimate stress'), a footnote, not a rule statement.

new_statements.quote: The LD group reflects the situation that holds in the majority of NENA: as a general rule, lexical stress is penultimate. [...] In LD, lexical stress is characterised by an increase in intensity, and frequently in pitch. In open accented syllables, moreover, all vowel except [ə] are long—above 95 ms. [...] As discussed below, however, there are several environments which prevent stress from being penultimate. [sec. 3.2.3:] In verbal forms except the Imperative, penultimate stress is blocked by the presence of the unstressable and semi-clitic suffixes: the L-series, and the -wa suffix [...]. In such cases, lexical accent falls as close to the penultimate syllable as possible (Rule 1a)

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate: penultimate stress) and as the existing statement from Molin's 2021 Cambridge PhD (sec. 2.3.2.1), of which this Brill grammar is the published revision; the 2024 chapter restates the penultimate default with the same phonetic characterisation (intensity, pitch, >95 ms open-syllable vowels) and adds an explicit rule system for the non-penultimate cases (Rules 1a/1b/1c), compensatory penultimate lengthening analysed as secondary stress (Rule 2), pretonic length retention (Rule 3), numeral/teen stress, and pausal retraction. It also generalises the statement from J. Dohok to the LD (Lishana Deni) group as a whole.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default lexical stress in J. Dohok (and the Lishana Deni group generally) is on the penultimate syllable, regular in nominals and independent numerals; stressed open-syllable vowels other than schwa are long. Departures are morphologically conditioned: (Rule 1a) in verbs the L-suffixes and -wa are unstressable semi-clitics, so stress falls as close to the penult as possible, i.e. on the syllable before them ('stress has to remain on a syllable that contains a radical of the verbal base', after Khan 2008b), which can put stress on the initial syllable of Past-based forms; 2pl -etun keeps stress on its first syllable; (Rule 1b) the enclitic 3rd-person present copula is invisible to stress, so stress is penultimate within the host; (Rule 1c) imperatives have fixed initial stress; teens are one phonological word stressed on the last syllable of the unit numeral; numerals modifying a noun may carry the more prominent stress (focal). Epenthetic schwa is invisible to stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Rule 2' - when stress cannot be penultimate (Rules 1a/1b/1c), the vowel of an open penultimate syllable is lengthened, 'lending the penultimate (i.e. canonically stress-bearing) syllable prominence to compensate for its lack of stress. This type of prominence can be considered secondary stress' (also operates across host+enclitic copula 'as if the entire construction were a single phonological word'); fn 21 notes this lengthening is not discussed in earlier LD studies. 'Rule 3': an open pretonic syllable that would bear stress without the L-/wa suffix keeps its long vowel (transcribed only for a).
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressable semi-clitic L-suffixes and -wa (stress on preceding syllable, Hoberman 1997 rule for J. Amediya said to hold for J. Dohok and apparently all LD); enclitic copula invisible to stress; imperative stress fixed on first syllable; -etun never stressed on its second syllable and its stressed vowel shortens to schwa before L-/wa in LD; teens stressed on the final syllable of the unit (ṭṃāné-ʾĕsar); neo-construct pal.gū́t keeps stress on what was the penult of the unapocopated form (surface final); a few pausal verbal forms show retracted, 'more archaic' stress ignoring L-suffix/wa (sec. 4); loanwords partly unadapted (sec. 3.2.2). Comparative note: peripheral Trans-Zab Jewish NENA and Mlaḥso have ultimate stress, unlike LD.
new_statements.identity_note: The chapter describes the Jewish NENA dialect of Dohok (J. Dohok) and explicitly extends the penultimate-stress statement to the whole Lishana Deni (LD) group (J. Zakho, J. Amediya, J. Betanure, J. Challa etc., citing Hoberman 1997, Mutzafi 2008a, Fassberg 2010), which is the glottocode's scope (lish1247 Lishana Deni); it contrasts LD with Trans-Zab Jewish NENA and Mlaḥso, which have ultimate stress and are different languages.
